answers.answer: Client sends /notes to gateway; gateway applies shared entrance policy, routes to Notes, and selects a Notes replica if it also balances load. Notes does the application work and returns its response through gateway to client. Routing selects Notes versus Authors; load balancing selects equivalent Notes instances. One product can do both. HTTPS method/path and body inspection require decrypted HTTP, so terminate client TLS at gateway, then separately protect the service hop with TLS and validate its certificate. Reject oversize requests before forwarding using a bounded check, not unlimited buffering. Note-specific business validation depends on application data and belongs in Notes.

evidence.quote: The request travels client → gateway → selected service.
A gateway product can do both, so two separate boxes are not always needed.
For HTTPS, method/path routing and body inspection need decrypted HTTP.
Enforce a bounded size check rather than buffering an unlimited body first.
Application rules that depend on business data belong with the service.

answers.answer: Authentication validates credentials to identify Alice; authorization determines whether Alice may read this note. Gateway must validate credentials rather than trust a presented token/header, remove or replace the claimed Bob identity with validated Alice identity. Notes must receive identity through a protected path authenticating the gateway and verify the forwarded assertion; encryption alone is insufficient. Block direct external Notes access or enforce equivalent identity and policy checks there. Notes checks Alice permission against its application data for Bob private note; being authenticated gives no blanket access.

evidence.quote: Receiving a token or identity header is not itself validation.
Remove or replace client-supplied identity claims with the validated identity.
A backend must accept that identity only through a protected path that authenticates the gateway; forwarded identity assertions must be verifiable by the backend.
Block direct external access to the backend, or enforce equivalent identity and policy checks on that path.
The service must check her permission for that resource against its application data.

answers.answer: Scope is one validated user across both gateway replicas, with at most 100 accepted requests in a stated minute period. Independent allowances let that user get 100 through each, or 200 total. Throttling limits rate; a burst is a short surge and best-effort throttling can exceed a target. A strict quota accounts for the shared allowance over the period and needs coordinated admission to prevent double spending across replicas. Coordination adds latency or an accounting dependency whose unavailability may require refusal. On 429 respect any retry delay, wait and bound retries. Counts do not measure query cost; expensive Notes queries or a shared database may still overload.

evidence.quote: Scope specifies which callers and gateway instances share a limit.
Sending traffic to both can admit 200.
Best-effort throttling may permit bursts or exceed a target; it is not strict quota accounting.
A strict shared allowance needs coordinated admission so replicas cannot spend the same allowance twice.
Coordination adds latency or a dependency that may require refusing work when accounting is unavailable.
On a 429 Too Many Requests response, respect any supplied retry delay; wait and bound retries instead of repeating immediately.
an expensive query costs more than a small read, and a shared database can still overload.

answers.answer: Gateway service wait must be shorter than the remaining two-second overall budget to reserve processing and response time. Retries and delays share that remaining budget. Timeout means no successful response arrived in time; client cannot infer whether creation committed. It does not cancel in-flight work or undo the committed note. Three client attempts times three gateway attempts can yield nine backend attempts. Choose client as retry owner, gateway forwards once, with at most three total client attempts and delays only while remaining budget permits. Reuse a stable operation ID for this one create across all attempts. Notes owns the effect and uses a durable record shared across replicas keyed by caller and operation ID; in one transaction uniquely reserve key, create note, record result, and commit all or none. Concurrent duplicates cannot reserve twice; completed duplicates return recorded result. Separate writes risk a crash gap. Gateway-only key/record cannot enforce the service transaction; new keys prevent repeat recognition.

evidence.quote: Retry attempts and their delays spend the same remaining budget; each attempt does not get a fresh two seconds.
The outcome is unknown to the client.
Timing out does not by itself cancel in-flight work or undo a committed write.
Three total client attempts, each causing three gateway attempts, can reach the backend nine times.
Choose one retry owner; other layers forward each attempt once.
Service replicas can share a durable database record keyed by caller and operation ID.
In one transaction, reserve that key uniquely, apply the effect and record its result; commit all or none.
Completed repeats return the recorded result.
A gateway-only record does not coordinate the service transaction.
A fresh key on every retry defeats duplicate recognition.

answers.answer: Aggregation combines Notes and Authors responses into one client response; fan-out is the multiple backend calls. Client makes fewer calls but backend work remains and additional dependencies can delay/fail the result. Choose two seconds overall, stop waiting on optional Authors at 500 ms, reserve time to return required Notes data, and explicitly mark display names missing rather than claim completeness. Allocate Notes a wait within the same overall deadline. If required Notes fails or misses its allocated deadline, fail the overview rather than invent or hide missing note data.

evidence.quote: Aggregation combines several backend responses into one client response.
Fan-out means making those multiple backend calls.
The client makes fewer calls, but backend work remains and the response depends on more services.
With two seconds total, stop waiting for optional data after 500 milliseconds and leave time to return the response.
Mark missing data explicitly rather than claiming completeness.
If required data misses its allocated deadline, fail the response instead of inventing it or disguising its absence.

answers.answer: An adequate single API already enforcing checks and limits may not need a separate gateway. Shared routing and entrance policies across several services can justify it. It adds a network hop and latency plus configuration and operating responsibility, and becomes a common failure point. A reachable alternate gateway and sufficient surviving gateway AND backend headroom are needed after failure; test failover reachability and observe latency, rejections and backend errors. More gateways cannot add saturated database capacity, fix a routing rule shared by replicas, or supply Notes resource authorization checks.

evidence.quote: A single API can enforce its own identity checks, permissions and request limits.
Shared routing and policies across several services can justify a separate gateway, but add a network hop, configuration and operating responsibility.
Surviving a gateway failure requires a reachable alternate gateway and enough surviving gateway and backend capacity, not just another box in the diagram.
More gateways do not fix that shared failure, create capacity in a saturated database or supply missing resource permission checks.
Test the reachable failover path and watch latency, rejections and backend errors.
